This page concerns the exact U.S. O*NET/SOC 11-3051.00 occupation, Industrial Production Managers: planning, directing, or coordinating the work activities and resources necessary for manufacturing products in accordance with cost, quality, and quantity specifications. Original official scope: Plan, direct, or coordinate the work activities and resources necessary for manufacturing products in accordance with cost, quality, and quantity specifications. U.S. wage and employment data on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS employment projections for 2024–2034 presented by O*NET (exact 11-3051.00 occupation scope). Exact occupational wages for mainland China have not been obtained and are recorded as a visible gap; the two jurisdictions and safety systems cannot be applied interchangeably.

To assess whether industrial production management suits you, first conduct a verifiable management exercise using public or simulated materials. Set up a fictional production scenario (for example, a production line with tight delivery deadlines and a rising defect rate). Write a step-by-step process from clarifying cost, quality, and quantity goals, checking production schedules and staffing, examining raw material and work-in-progress quality, consulting technical or administrative staff to resolve production problems, and deciding schedule and resource adjustments, through to preparing production and personnel reports and reporting to management. Mark checkpoints and potential problems at each step (schedule and budget conflicts, unmet quality or safety requirements, insufficient staffing or skills, equipment or material shortages, and personnel actions crossing labor-law boundaries). Then check whether cost-quality-quantity tradeoffs, safety and compliance requirements, and personnel and authorization boundaries are treated as indispensable; whether major investment, safety determinations, and legal decisions beyond your authority are framed as requests for approval or referrals; and whether decision grounds and records are retained for review. Test this through actual deliverables rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire.

Fit signals | Tasks and work activities in U.S. O*NET 11-3051.00 show that this occupation primarily involves setting and monitoring product standards; directing or coordinating production, processing, and distribution; reviewing processing schedules or production orders and deciding inventory requirements and staffing within budget and time constraints; reviewing operations and consulting technical or administrative staff to resolve production problems; hiring, training, evaluating, or handling personnel grievances; developing production tracking or quality control systems; preparing production and personnel reports; and participating in the development of new products or processes. Work centers on data monitoring, cross-department consultation, and team management, with frequent communication and responsibility for others' health, safety, and results. The interest code is ECR (Enterprising–Conventional–Realistic); key skills include critical thinking, monitoring, speaking, and judgment and decision making. If you are willing to organize resources, lead teams, and take responsibility for production results within cost, quality, and quantity constraints, these everyday demands are closer to your way of working.

Caution signals | The official scope and tasks involve production goals, personnel and equipment, and safety and personnel matters. An undetected schedule-budget conflict, an unmet quality standard or safety requirement, insufficient staffing or skills, a personnel action crossing labor-law boundaries, or a major investment or safety decision beyond one's authority can cause delivery failure, financial loss, or personal-safety and compliance risks. This page therefore lists cost-quality-quantity tradeoffs, safety and compliance requirements, personnel and labor-law boundaries, and authorization boundaries separately. In the U.S., the occupation itself is not marked Bright Outlook. The O*NET summary and employment trends indicate below-average projected growth (2%) for 2024–2034, approximately 17,100 job openings annually, and approximately 241,900 workers employed in 2024. If intensive communication, tradeoffs among multiple goals, and responsibility for personnel are difficult for you to bear, treat these as practical costs that require careful consideration.

Assessing responsibility | Genuine fit depends on whether you can do three things together in the same management task: ground production and data in solid work (set and monitor standards, review schedules and orders, analyze operating reports, and prepare production and personnel records to provide reviewable grounds for decisions); manage standards and safety (quality and safety requirements, cost and budget constraints, labor law and personnel standards, following institutional and regulatory requirements); and assume definable management responsibility (answer for your own decisions and team results, and request approval or refer major investments, safety determinations, and legal decisions beyond your authority). Test this through a verifiable experience, such as completing a step-by-step production management plan and decision record, or practicing schedule and quality tradeoffs with simulated operating data, rather than relying solely on interest-questionnaire conclusions.

Industrial production managers' daily work can be divided into three strands: (1) goals and monitoring—set and monitor product standards, review processing schedules or production orders, and analyze operating reports to identify production problems; (2) resources and coordination—decide inventory requirements, staffing, and workflows within budget and time constraints, and consult technical or administrative staff to resolve production problems; (3) teams and reporting—hire, train, and evaluate employees, handle personnel grievances, prepare production and personnel records, and report to management. All three strands share the same cost, quality, and quantity requirements, but their outputs differ: goals and monitoring focus on standards, resources and coordination on execution, and teams and reporting on personnel and management.

O*NET 11-3051.00, Industrial Production Managers: plan, direct, or coordinate the work activities and resources necessary for manufacturing products in accordance with cost, quality, and quantity specifications. Core tasks include setting and monitoring product standards; directing and coordinating production, processing, distribution, and marketing activities; reviewing schedules and orders and making decisions within budget and time constraints; reviewing operations and consulting to resolve production problems; managing personnel; developing production tracking or quality control systems; and preparing production and personnel reports. Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed), with an SVP range from 7.0 to below 8.0.

subject.name: Industrial Production Managers
subject.summary: Industrial production managers correspond to the exact U.S. O*NET/SOC 11-3051.00 occupation, Industrial Production Managers: they plan, direct, or coordinate the work activities and resources necessary for manufacturing products in accordance with cost, quality, and quantity specifications. Original official scope: Plan, direct, or coordinate the work activities and resources necessary for manufacturing products in accordance with cost, quality, and quantity specifications. Core tasks include setting and monitoring product standards; directing and coordinating production, processing, distribution, and marketing activities; reviewing processing schedules or production orders and deciding inventory requirements and staffing within budget and time constraints; reviewing operations and consulting to resolve production problems; managing personnel; developing production tracking or quality control systems; and preparing production and personnel reports. U.S. wages on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 data presented by O*NET (median annual wage USD 126,060, median hourly wage USD 60.61); employment and outlook come from BLS employment projections for 2024–2034 (approximately 241,900 workers in 2024, below-average growth of 2%, and approximately 17,100 openings annually). All use the exact 11-3051.00 occupation scope. Exact occupational wages for mainland China have not been obtained and are recorded as a visible gap; Chinese qualification, safety, and labor-system boundaries are marked separately.
